rationale: The ledger is unchanged since the incumbent (same evidence records GEO-E001–E036), but the panel is contested — four of five seats dispute the case verdict and five of five dispute GEO-C020 — so a complete assessment is returned and every dissent is answered here. CASE VERDICT — Gemini and Grok (contradicted), GPT (mixed), Opus (weakly_supported): HOLD unresolved. The thesis GEO-C022 is existential; its Egyptian instance is now graded contradicted (below), but its Andean instance has never been examined by anyone outside the proponent team, and GEO-E008 is a 1971 sandstone-provenance study that neither tests the andesite nor can exclude same-quarry aggregate. 'Contradicted' would require a negative record on Pumapunku stone; none exists. 'Mixed' would require a genuine evidential collision within the thesis; Egypt-negative and Andes-untested is not a collision but an incomplete test. 'Weakly_supported' would require the surviving positive line to move the prior; GEO-E006/E007 are one team, one sample set, contested custody, and of exactly the type (SEM microstructure read as artificial) that GEO-E020's positive control showed to be non-diagnostic at Giza. The decisive test has been run at the wrong site — that is unresolved as a finding, not a default. GEO-C022 — same seats, same answer: HOLD. GEO-C020 — ADOPT contradicted (all five seats). Decided by GEO-E020: the only study with a genuine Davidovits geopolymer as positive control found the alkali/Al binder enrichment and air-void matrix a real casting binder leaves absent from every casing stone, and Barsoum's Si-rich spheres present in natural limestone; reinforced by GEO-E018 (in-situ bedding, burrows, fossil cross-sections, block-confined tectonic fractures), GEO-E019 and GEO-E021. The incumbent's weakly_supported treated an untested residue (the C–S–H binder of GEO-E017) as support; absence of a test is not support. GEO-E017 remains the strongest objection and carries the steelman. Confidence moderate because of the sample-identity dispute and the untested recipe. GEO-C021 — ADOPT weakly_supported (Gemini, GPT, Grok, Opus); HOLD against GLM (unresolved). GEO-E006/E007 are the only records on the monument stone itself and support; GEO-E008 is on a different lithology with pre-modern methods. The incumbent's own synthesis called this 'an untested branch, not a genuine evidential collision', which is inconsistent with 'mixed'. The ledger is not silent, so not unresolved; it is one non-independent line, so weakly_supported at low confidence. GEO-C003 — ADOPT contradicted (Gemini, GPT, Grok, Opus), confidence low. Decided by GEO-E027 (the compilation of the principal medieval accounts describes the breach twice in detail with no salt) together with GEO-E029 (the only carrier cites no author and misdates the event). Unread Arabic sources (GEO-R001) are the route to reversal and are named in whatWouldChangeOurMind. GEO-C506 — ADOPT contradicted (same four seats). Decided by GEO-E031 (halite efflorescence at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites) and GEO-E032 (halite reported as a primary constituent of Giza nummulitic limestone). The claim's content is the comparison, and the comparators that matter carry the salt; GEO-E030 confirms presence only, which is not what the claim distinctively asserts. Confidence moderate because no concentration comparison exists (GEO-R010). GEO-C011 — ADOPT established (Gemini, Grok, GLM, Opus): GEO-E010 is a strong mainstream record whose statements the claim closely tracks; GEO-E011 supplies the analytical basis. GEO-C907 — ADOPT established (Gemini, GPT): GEO-E030 quotes the peer-reviewed paper, read in full via PMC, and the claim is scoped to the reported result. GEO-C001 — ADOPT well_supported (Grok, GLM); HOLD against established (Gemini, GPT): a single unreplicated team and configuration (GEO-E001 limitations); GEO-R002 is the replication. GEO-C004 — ADOPT well_supported (GLM, Opus); HOLD against established (Gemini, GPT): the papers' citations were confirmed but the source records show their content was characterised from the Davidovits 2024 bibliography, not read directly. HOLD against Grok (weakly_supported): that grades the interpretation, which lives in GEO-C021; the claim as worded is a report of what was published. GEO-C903 — HOLD well_supported against established (Gemini, GPT, Grok): GEO-E035 is abstract-only, the PDF returned 403, so the model's body was not read. GEO-C906 — HOLD provisionally_supported against Gemini (established) and Opus (well_supported): GEO-E032 is a second-hand citation of Klemm & Klemm, unread, and the 'inherent' inference rests on detached fragments; GEO-R010 is the test. GEO-C594 — HOLD provisionally_supported against Gemini/Grok (well_supported) and GPT (weakly_supported): GEO-E034 is one moderate record at one monument; it establishes the confound at the flagship site but not the general quantifier, which awaits GEO-R005. GEO-C012 — HOLD provisionally_supported against Gemini (well_supported) and GPT (weakly_supported): a real artificial limestone exists in the record (GEO-E020's positive control) and the C–S–H chemistry is demonstrated (GEO-E022), but 'large' and 'ancient inputs only' rest on self-report (GEO-E013). GEO-C010 — HOLD against Gemini/Opus (well_supported) and GPT/Grok (weakly_supported): the ledger alone is one weak proponent record (GEO-E016), which would warrant weakly_supported; the verdict rests on a declared prior about Bronze Age pyrotechnology, stated in the reasoning. Not a split: the two components (ledger, prior) are named and the verdict follows from combining them. GEO-C030 — HOLD mixed against Gemini (contradicted) and GLM (well_supported): the claim bundles a true proposition (PXRF/ICP-MS blind to H/C/O; a quarry match is not a proof of carving — GEO-E024, GEO-E035) with a false one (XRD listed as blind) and an overreach (GEO-E020 shows binder-aware methods see binders). Mixed is the finding, not the default. GEO-C013 — HOLD weakly_supported against Grok/Opus (unresolved): one weak supporting record (GEO-E015), none against; that is weak support, not an undecidable question. GEO-C006 — HOLD weakly_supported against Opus (unresolved): same logic on GEO-E005; the competing proponent reading Opus cites bears on diagnosticity, which is graded low. GEO-C005 — HOLD weakly_supported against GPT/Opus (unresolved): the claim as worded is that an argument has been made (GEO-E014); its merit is where doubt lives, and that is graded through low diagnosticity and low confidence rather than by moving the credibility verdict. GEO-C502 — HOLD weakly_supported against Gemini/Grok/GLM (provisionally_supported): the only carrier is Fóti's characterisation, unverified against the monograph (GEO-E002 limitation), and the source record notes three other Fóti characterisations found inaccurate. SELECTION: the featured set of 20 is unchanged; no unfeatured claim carries evidence. CRUX ORDER: reordered so the Andean checks lead (GEO-R009, GEO-R012) because with the Egyptian branch contradicted the case verdict now turns on Pumapunku, and both are legible without touching a monument; GEO-R011 follows as the recipe-independent Egyptian test. ARTICLE: rewritten to carry the new verdicts — the salt section now states that the medieval report is contradicted on what has been read and that the comparative salt claim fails; the Egypt section concludes 'contradicted' with the C–S–H residue as objection; the Andes section is reframed as the branch the case rests on, with the Giza positive-control precedent as the specific reason for caution; the ladder and closing distinguish the resolved instance from the unresolved thesis.
article:
At the granite quarries of Aswan, beside the largest abandoned obelisk in Egypt, there is a block that tourists are invited to hit. The idea is charming: pick up one of the rounded dolerite stones that ancient workers supposedly used, strike the granite, and feel the past in your hands. Guides have been running this accidental experiment for decades. According to the proponent literature, [no visitor has ever managed to reproduce one of the smooth, scooped depressions that cover the quarry walls]{claim=GEO-C002}. The stones bounce. The granite shrugs.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P01}

Anecdotes like this prove nothing by themselves, and this one has never been systematically surveyed — nobody has counted the attempts, weighed the effort, or examined the test block for wear. But it points at the right question, which is not *who built the monuments* — nobody serious disputes that ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and ancient Andeans built Tiwanaku — but *how the hardest stone was worked*. The megalithic casting hypothesis gives a heterodox answer: some of it was not worked at all. It was made — mixed, moulded, and set in place, the way we make concrete — from crushed or gathered rock, a mineral binder, and chemistry that a Bronze Age society could plausibly command.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P02}

The idea has a serious pedigree and a disreputable neighbourhood. It was put in scientific form by the French materials chemist Joseph Davidovits, whose group has since published in peer-reviewed materials journals, and it has attracted at least one laboratory with no stake in the theory. It also circulates in a media ecosystem of lost civilisations and ancient high technology that this case has nothing to do with. Casting requires no aliens, no Atlantis, and no forgotten machines — only forgotten chemistry, which is a documented historical phenomenon. That is what makes it testable. And it has been tested — at one monument thoroughly, at another not at all. The two records are different, and the difference is the whole story.

## The conventional account, taken seriously

Any honest map of this dispute starts by steelmanning the orthodoxy, because the orthodoxy is strong.

The carved-and-transported account is not a guess. Quarries exist, with unfinished monuments still attached to bedrock — the Aswan obelisk itself is the most famous, abandoned mid-extraction after the granite cracked. Tools have been recovered in quantity. Worker settlements at Giza have been excavated. Experimental archaeologists have carved granite with dolerite and copper, slowly but genuinely. And modern geochemical provenancing has matched monument stone to specific quarries. The cleanest example is Stonehenge: immobile-trace-element analysis finds that fifty of fifty-two sarsens share a single geochemical profile, and Stone 58's signature directly matches the West Woods area about 25 km away — not a loose statistical resemblance but a match.

The conventional account's gaps are quantitative, not existential. It needs no miracle anywhere. What it needs, in a few specific places, is more time, more workers, or better technique than anyone has yet demonstrated. Those places are where this case lives.

## Where the anomalies actually are

Strip away everything anecdotal and the residue is small but real. It comes in three kinds: rates, ingredients, and the record. A fourth — the salt on the pyramid's walls — gets its own section, because it is the anomaly on which the evidence is thick enough to reach a conclusion.

### Rates

For a century the standard account of granite quarrying rested largely on Reginald Engelbach's 1922 report on the Aswan obelisk. Proponents characterise [its experimental basis as a single self-conducted one-hour trial with no measurement of the mass removed, and its workforce figure as a count-divided-by-four heuristic]{claim=GEO-C502}; that characterisation is theirs and has not been checked against the monograph — and the same author's characterisations of three other sources have been found to differ from the originals — so hold it loosely. In 2023 a team finally produced a modern number: [photogrammetric measurement of granite removal with a dolerite pounder gave roughly 216 cubic centimetres per hour at 85 strikes a minute]{claim=GEO-C001} — a rate the authors themselves say speaks against pounders as the *sole* quarrying method. That is a peer-reviewed measurement, from a single team, and it is the most mainstream-legible item in the anomaly column.

Note carefully what it is evidence *for*. It stresses the orthodox timeline. It says nothing about casting: fire-setting, chisels, or simply more labour would each absorb the shortfall without a single mould. The same goes for the quarry's stranger features — [vertical shafts some five metres deep, described as too narrow for a worker to swing a pounder at their bottom]{claim=GEO-C006} — which have not been surveyed by anyone without a stake in the answer.

### Ingredients

The natron-route version of the hypothesis, developed by the researcher Marcell Fóti, starts from a fact that is not in dispute: Egypt sat on [industrial-scale deposits of natron — the alkaline salt ancient glassmakers used as a flux — exploited from antiquity, with supply declining sharply in the seventh to ninth centuries AD]{claim=GEO-C011}. Natron plus heat plus silica gives waterglass, a mineral binder, and [the roughly 850 °C required was within reach of charcoal-and-bellows pyrotechnology]{claim=GEO-C010} — a point the record supports only through a proponent's citation of early glassmaking, though what is known of ancient metallurgy makes it hard to doubt. Crucible-scale heat, however, is not industrial-scale processing, and the natron papers concern glass and faience; they say nothing about stone. The proposed discovery story — that [long-used outdoor fire pits accidentally produce hardened artificial stone through ash chemistry]{claim=GEO-C013} — rests on one unattributed anecdote and has never been replicated.

All of this is necessary for casting and none of it is evidence of casting. Ingredients on the shelf do not make a cake.

### The record

{plate:IMG-GEO-P05}

The historical anchors are thin. In the Tomb of Rekhmire an 18th-Dynasty mural shows a large casting operation — rows of crucibles tended by workers with poles. Egyptology reads it as bronze casting. Fóti argues that [the scale and apparatus depicted fit mineral or waterglass processing better than bronze work]{claim=GEO-C005}. That is an interpretive argument by a proponent that conventional Egyptology has not engaged; a serious re-reading would ask what residues or tools each interpretation predicts in the archaeological record, and go and look.

## The salt

The proponents' favourite historical anchor is a story about the Caliph al-Maʾmūn. When his party broke into the Great Pyramid in the ninth century, the story goes, [it found the interior chamber walls coated with a layer of salt]{claim=GEO-C003} — a centimetre and a half of cooking salt, in the Geopolymer Institute's telling. Salt is an odd thing for a sealed structure of dry quarried limestone to produce, and an expected residue of stone that set wet with natron in it. The Institute adds a modern coda: on four visits between 1984 and 2003 Davidovits picked up fragments at Giza and found them salty to the tongue, European cathedrals are not salt-encrusted, and so [Great Pyramid stone carries surface salt that comparable natural limestone does not]{claim=GEO-C506}.

Take the medieval story first. The principal Arabic accounts of the breach were gathered in the fifteenth century by al-Suyūṭī, whose compilation exists in Leon Nemoy's 1939 translation. It tells the story twice, and in detail. The workers kindled fire, applied vinegar, tempered iron tools and brought up catapults; they found the wall twenty cubits thick; behind it a jar holding a thousand dinars, a square well with doors onto chambers of shrouded corpses, a narrow shaft of black quartz, a covered granite basin in which they found “nothing but worn out pieces of rope”. Not one of these passages mentions salt, halite, or any coating on the walls. The web page that carries the salt report names no medieval author, work or manuscript for it. Even its date is unsupported: the translator places the caliph's arrival in Egypt, to suppress a rebellion, in AH 217 — that is AD 832, not the 820 the page gives. Other medieval authors remain to be read, and a single located passage would revive the story. But on what has been read, the claim that the accounts report salt is not merely unproven: the accounts that exist do not report it, and the only text that says they do cites nothing. We grade it contradicted, with low confidence, and name the unread authors as the way to reverse that.

Now the modern salt — which turns out to be real. A conservation study by the ScanPyramids mission, published in *Scientific Reports* in 2026, examined efflorescence (the white crust that forms when dissolved salts migrate to a surface and crystallise) inside the Queen's Chamber and the so-called Thieves' Corridor. [X-ray diffraction of seven samples found only halite, calcite and quartz; electron microscopy of the white crust detected only sodium and chlorine, growing as tiny whiskers; there were no nitrates and no widespread gypsum]{claim=GEO-C907}. So the taste test was right about one thing. The salt on the pyramid's inner walls is common salt.

What the study does not show is that the salt is anomalous. The same paper lists halite as a dominant efflorescence salt at limestone monuments across Egypt — the Menkaure pyramid, the Saqqara pyramid, the White Monastery at Sohag, the Imni tomb at Lisht, and the Sphinx, which is carved from Giza bedrock and which nobody claims was cast. And it cites the geologists Klemm and Klemm for the view that [halite is a primary constituent of the plateau's nummulitic limestone, present within the strata themselves and precipitated from evaporating marine or lagoonal waters when the rock formed]{claim=GEO-C906}. That citation is second-hand — the book has not been read for this case — and no one has compared salt concentrations between pyramid stone and unworked bedrock, or tested whether the salt runs through the body of a block or sits on its skin. But the natron recipe predicts salt in the blocks, and so does ordinary quarrying of a salt-bearing marine limestone. An observation both accounts predict cannot decide between them. The proponents' comparator — cathedrals — is a different rock in a different climate; the comparators that matter are the plateau's own bedrock and its neighbours, and those carry the salt. The comparative claim fails on the record as it stands.

There is a further complication that cuts deeper than the salt. The same study reports that [conservation work inside the pyramid between 1995 and 1997 is undocumented — photographs show that surfaces were cleaned and cavities filled, a sulfur-rich modern fill sits on the chamber wall, and salt that was barely visible in 2022 had spread extensively across the stone two years later]{claim=GEO-C594}. Every surface-salt observation at Giza, including four decades of tasting, is therefore a reading taken at an unknown point in a cleaning cycle whose baseline nobody recorded. That problem is not peculiar to the salt. It hangs over every surface argument at every megalithic site, almost none of which has a complete published restoration history — though that generalisation, unlike the Giza instance, has yet to be audited.

What survives of the salt line is a narrow, cheap question: does unworked Giza and Mokattam bedrock, and the quarry face at Tura, effloresce halite? If yes — as the plateau's geology predicts — the salt argument is finished. If no, the salt becomes an anomaly worth testing in the bulk of the stone rather than on its surface.

## The stone itself

Everything above is circumstantial. The case turns on what the monument stone is actually made of, and here two branches have very different records.

### Egypt: tested, and contradicted

{plate:IMG-GEO-P03}

The pyramid claim is that [some blocks of the Great Pyramid — not the core, but casing, tops, and backing blocks — are cast reconstituted limestone rather than quarried natural stone]{claim=GEO-C020}. Two laboratory results point that way. In 2006 a Drexel University group compared pyramid limestone under electron microscopy with six natural limestones from the area and reported microconstituents combining silicon, calcium, and magnesium “in ratios that do not exist in any of the potential limestone sources”, along with hydrated phases “not known to hydrate in nature” — while conceding that nature “could have — however unlikely — produced all the microstructures examined”. In 2011 an overlapping team applied solid-state NMR to a casing stone from the Bent Pyramid at Dahshur and read it as Tura limestone grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel “formed by human intervention”, perhaps with diatomaceous earth added.

Notice the second result quietly changes the recipe. Davidovits proposed an alkali-aluminosilicate geopolymer; the NMR study proposes a lime-pozzolan cement — the chemistry of a mortar, not of a geopolymer. That matters for how the negatives count.

And the negatives are substantial. Four independent petrographic examinations — petrography is the study of stone under a microscope, the geologist's basic tool — every one concluding natural limestone. Folk and Campbell, working across many blocks in the field, report sedimentary bedding, burrows, sharp cross-sections of clams and fragile worm tubes, ripple lamination, and calcite-filled tectonic fractures confined to individual blocks — features that geology produces and moulds do not. Harrell and Penrod examined the “Lauer sample”, the pyramid-interior specimen proponents cite as their showcase, and found natural Mokattam limestone with “no evidence of the special textures and zeolite cement that must exist if the sample is concrete”. Freestone and Middleton ran five techniques on a British Museum casing fragment and found no feature supporting an artificial origin; the cristobalite that Davidovits once treated as a synthetic marker turned out to be opal-CT, a normal sedimentary product. And Jana did the one thing nobody else in this literature has done: he examined casing stones side by side with natural Tura limestone *and* a genuine Davidovits-made geopolymer block — a positive control, the specimen that shows what the signature looks like when it is really there. The silicon-rich spheres highlighted in 2006 appeared in casing stones and natural limestone alike. The geopolymer showed a binder heavily enriched in sodium, potassium, and aluminium that no casing stone showed. The artificial block had a smooth matrix with spherical air voids; the monument stone and the quarry stone shared a grainy texture with pores between the grains.

Weigh the whole. Every examination of Great Pyramid stone by anyone outside the proponent camp reads it as natural, and the one with a positive control shows that the features proponents called artificial occur in undisputed quarry stone, while the features a real binder leaves do not occur in the monument. On this record the claim that some Great Pyramid blocks are cast is contradicted. Two things stop that from being the end of the matter. One is a fight over the samples themselves. Davidovits contends the piece his critics analysed was not the authentic Lauer sample — wrong thickness, missing phosphate coating — though Jana reports finding and mapping that very coating on the piece he received. Egypt's antiquities authority, for its part, states that no sampling permission was ever granted for the 2006 study and that its samples' origin is unknown. The other is the recipe. Jana's decisive negative is a negative for the *alkali* recipe; it does not test the calcium-silicate binder of the 2011 NMR study, which has drawn no published rebuttal and which, at a few per cent by weight, might hide from bulk chemistry. That residue is what a proponent can still honestly point to. It is an objection to the verdict, not evidence against it: nothing in the record has looked for that binder and found it, either.

### The Andes: the branch the case rests on

{plate:IMG-GEO-P04}

At Pumapunku in Bolivia the laboratory evidence is the only kind from a disputed monument that reads as artificial. [Published SEM and petrographic analyses of the andesite report organic matter and microstructural features the authors argue natural volcanic stone should not contain]{claim=GEO-C004}, and on that basis the claim is that [some andesite and red sandstone blocks at Pumapunku and Tiwanaku were geopolymer-cast]{claim=GEO-C021}. Those papers passed peer review in materials journals, and nothing in the record has been aimed directly against them — no independent laboratory has re-examined the stone. That makes the claim weakly supported: the only direct evidence on the stone itself points toward casting. Three cautions keep it weak. The papers come from one team — the Davidovits group — analysing one sample set whose chain of custody is contested. Volcanic rocks host glassy and organic phases naturally, and the criteria for telling natural from artificial were never blind-tested. And there is the Giza precedent: when features of exactly this kind — microstructures read as artificial under the electron microscope — were checked against a genuine geopolymer, they turned out to occur in natural limestone too. Nobody has run that check on andesite.

The standing counter-evidence is a 1971 Bolivian Academy of Sciences study attributing Pumapunku's red sandstones to identifiable natural quarries. It is a provenance study of sandstone set against microscopy of andesite, so the two partly talk past each other. The proponents' current model is more specific than it used to be, and therefore more checkable. [It holds that the andesite was cast from natural, uncrushed volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia — a material like the Roman pozzolana — carried to and stored at the lakeshore village of Iwawe, where it forms Stratum V of a 2002 excavation, and that the abandoned quadrangular blocks called *piedras cansadas*, “tired stones”, were never used as building material]{claim=GEO-C903}. Both the orthodox account and the proponents agree the andesite comes from Khapia, so quarry geochemistry cannot separate them. A lakeshore deposit, a mountain, and some abandoned blocks can. Reading the excavators' own description of Stratum V is desk work; walking Khapia's outcrops for working faces and dressing debris — or for loose sand and none — is a field season.

### Can it be done at all?

The one rung of the ladder in decent shape is the humblest: [limestone can be reconstituted into large, hard blocks visually similar to natural stone with materials and temperatures available to ancient builders]{claim=GEO-C012}. Davidovits' institute reports multi-ton demonstration blocks, self-reported and never independently analysed; lime and diatomaceous earth form a calcium-silicate gel at room temperature in the laboratory; and the geopolymer block Jana examined is, after all, a real artificial limestone — distinguishable under the microscope, which is the point, but a stone. Feasibility is not occurrence. But it is not nothing either, and it is the reason this case is a question and not a fantasy.

## The ladder, and why it thins as it climbs

Notice the shape. At the bottom: observations, some solid, most unverified. In the middle: mechanism claims — the ingredients existed, the temperatures were reachable, the chemistry works. At the top: the claim that actually matters, that [at least one major megalithic monument, somewhere, contains man-made cast stone]{claim=GEO-C022}. Each rung is weaker than the one below, and evidence for a lower rung does not automatically climb. Natron in Egypt is established and proves nothing about pyramids. Feasibility is real and proves nothing about history.

The headline claim is existential — *at least one* monument — so it cannot be settled by averaging. Egypt has been tested with binder-aware methods and, in the recipe tested, contradicted. The Andes have been examined by one interested team and by nobody else. An existential claim is not refuted by one failed instance, and it is not supported by an untested one. That is why the headline verdict is *unresolved*: not a shrug, but a description of a record in which the decisive test has been run at the wrong site.

## The crux

Here is where the disagreement lives, and it is narrower than either camp usually admits.

The strongest conventional evidence class is provenance matching: monument stone chemically fingerprinted to a quarry. The casting hypothesis's most consequential reply is methodological — [that trace-element quarry-matching methods are blind to hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen, and so cannot by design tell carved quarry stone from stone cast using aggregate gathered at that same quarry]{claim=GEO-C030}. Crushed rock keeps its metallic fingerprint. The narrow point is correct: portable XRF and ICP-MS do not see the light elements a binder is made of, and a quarry match is a quarry match, not a proof of carving. Even at Stonehenge, the West Woods result tells you where the sarsen came from, not how it was shaped. At Khapia it is exactly why the two sides cannot be separated by geochemistry.

But the reply reaches less far than its authors want. The claim lists X-ray diffraction among the blind methods, when XRD reads crystalline phases and is exactly how Folk and Campbell looked for zeolite cement. Fóti's own methods table lists NMR as blind to silicon and oxygen, when solid-state silicon NMR is exactly what the pro-casting Bent Pyramid study used. And the critique does not touch the direct petrography at all. Cast stone needs a binder; binders have signatures — bound water, alkali enrichment, textures geology does not produce. Jana's positive control demonstrates those signatures are plainly visible when present. A methods audit of the provenance literature is worth doing, and it would likely show that some “we found the quarry” conclusions have been stretched into “therefore carved” conclusions the chemistry cannot carry. It would not rescue a monument in which someone has looked directly for a binder and found none.

## What would change our mind

The strongest case for the hypothesis that this record does not answer is this: the revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for. The four negative Egyptian studies were built around the alkali recipe, and the one with a positive control used an alkali geopolymer as the control. A cement at five per cent by weight — exactly the kind the 2011 NMR study proposes and the 2010 laboratory work shows is easy to make — could sit inside a casing stone that reads as natural in every one of those tests. Nothing in the record rules that out, and the provenance critique means quarry matching cannot rule it out either.

The strongest case against is equally plain: every time monument stone has been examined directly for casting by anyone outside the proponent camp, it has read as natural — down to fossil worm tubes and tectonic fractures — the one historical anecdote proponents lean on has no traceable author, and the salt it describes is what the plateau's own rock is reported to shed.

So here is what would move us.

- **Toward casting:** an independent laboratory reproducing the Pumapunku organic and microstructural findings on samples with a documented chain of custody, against a natural andesite control; a provenance-secure Egyptian casing stone in which an independent lab finds a calcium-silicate cement absent from matched Tura limestone; a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many pyramid blocks, measured against the natural remanence of Mokattam quarry limestone, finding a shared magnetic direction aligned with the present field — something a block that set in place should carry regardless of recipe, and a quarried, rotated block should not; the Iwawe deposit turning out to be a natural andesite sand store dated to the construction period, with no extraction faces on Khapia; a medieval Arabic author who actually reports the salt.
- **Toward carving:** an independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite finding ordinary volcanic mineralogy, or its “artificial” features reproduced in undisputed volcanic rock; a targeted test for a calcium-silicate binder in provenance-secure casing stone returning nothing; halite effloresc­ing from unworked Giza bedrock, which would retire the salt argument entirely; the Iwawe deposit turning out to be dressing debris or unrelated fill, with quarry faces and carved andesite blocks documented on the way down from Khapia.

This case ends in two different places. On its most famous instance it reaches a conclusion: on the present record, the stone of the Great Pyramid reads as quarried, and the salt on its walls is what the plateau's own rock sheds. On its headline question it does not, because the one monument where the laboratory evidence points the other way has never been examined by anyone without a stake in the answer. The agenda that follows is therefore weighted toward the Andes, and much of it is cheap. Read the Iwawe excavation report. Walk Khapia's outcrops for quarry faces or for sand. Design the blinded paleomagnetic survey that tests set-in-place against quarried without arguing about recipes. Audit which provenance studies can, and cannot, see a binder. Test whether the plateau's bedrock effloresces salt. Finish tracing the salt story through the remaining medieval authors, or drop it. Audit the restoration histories that could account for any surface anomaly — starting with a pyramid interior that was cleaned in the 1990s and nobody wrote down how. Replicate the quarrying rate. Re-read the Rekhmire mural with a metallurgist and a chemist in the same room.

The scoop marks at Aswan have waited a very long time for someone to measure them properly. The full agenda, with what each project would tell us, is below.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis (GEO-C022) is existential — at least one monument — so the case verdict cannot be an average across branches, and it must be graded branch by branch. The Egyptian branch (GEO-C020) is the only one tested with binder-aware methods on monument stone, and it is contradicted: GEO-E018 (in-situ sedimentary bedding, burrows, fossil cross-sections and block-confined tectonic fractures across many blocks), GEO-E019 (the proponents' showcase Lauer sample reads as natural Mokattam limestone with no zeolite cement), GEO-E021 (an independent multi-technique study of a museum casing fragment finds natural limestone and opal-CT rather than synthetic cristobalite), and above all GEO-E020, whose genuine Davidovits-made positive control shows that a real alkali-aluminosilicate binder is plainly visible when present — Na+K and Al enrichment, smooth matrix with air voids — and absent from every casing stone examined, while the Si-rich spheres of GEO-E012 occur in natural limestone too. Against these stand GEO-E012 (contested provenance, features later matched in natural stone) and GEO-E017 (one Bent Pyramid casing stone read by NMR as Tura grains in a calcium-silicate gel, Barsoum co-author, no rebuttal). GEO-E017 is the surviving objection: its C–S–H binder is outside the scope of GEO-E020's alkali-specific negative, and GEO-E022 shows the chemistry is feasible. But no record has looked for that binder and found it, so it qualifies the confidence of the negative rather than supplying support. The salt line adds nothing: the medieval report (GEO-C003) is carried only by an uncited proponent page (GEO-E029) and is absent from al-Suyūṭī's compilation of the breach accounts (GEO-E027); the modern salt is confirmed as halite (GEO-E030) but halite effloresces at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites (GEO-E031) and is reported, second-hand via Klemm & Klemm, as a primary constituent of Giza limestone (GEO-E032), while undocumented 1990s cleaning leaves every surface observation without a baseline (GEO-E034); GEO-E033 therefore removes the salt as support for GEO-C020 without testing any block. The Andean branch (GEO-C021) is weakly supported: GEO-E006/GEO-E007 are the only records on the monument stone itself and read it as artificial, and nothing in the ledger tests them directly — GEO-E008 is a 1971 provenance study of sandstone set against microscopy of andesite and cannot in principle exclude same-quarry aggregate. They are one team, one sample set, contested custody, never independently rerun, and of exactly the type (SEM microstructure read as artificial) that GEO-E020's positive control found non-diagnostic at Giza. The proponents' 2020 model (GEO-E035) makes the branch checkable at Iwawe and Khapia without touching a monument. The methods critique (GEO-C030, GEO-E024) holds in its narrow form — light-element blindness is real for PXRF and ICP-MS and legitimately limits quarry-match reasoning such as GEO-E009 — but the claim wrongly lists XRD as blind and does not reach direct binder-aware petrography. The Aswan material (GEO-C001, GEO-C002, GEO-C006, GEO-C502) bears on the completeness of the pounding orthodoxy, not on casting. Why unresolved rather than contradicted, mixed or weakly supported: an existential claim is not refuted by one contradicted instance when the other instance has no negative record at all; Egypt-negative and Andes-untested is not an evidential collision; and a single non-independent positive of a type already shown non-diagnostic elsewhere does not move the prior. The decisive test has been run at the wrong site. The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is GEO-E020: without its positive control the Egyptian record would be two supportive and three negative studies with no demonstration that a casting signature is detectable at all, GEO-C020 would drift back toward mixed, and the proponents' blindness argument (GEO-C030) would stand unanswered against the petrography — moving the case toward mixed. With it, the Egyptian branch is contradicted in the tested recipe, and the case is unresolved only because the C–S–H variant and the Andean stone have never been independently examined.
assessment.steelman: The revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for, and the only monument whose stone reads as artificial in the laboratory has never been examined by anyone but its proponents. Every negative Egyptian study was built around Davidovits' alkali-aluminosilicate recipe; the one with a positive control (GEO-E020) used an alkali geopolymer as that control and its author concedes a binder at about 5 wt% might not register in bulk chemistry. GEO-E017 reports solid-state ²⁹Si/²⁷Al/⁴³Ca NMR on a Bent Pyramid casing stone reading as Tura grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel, with no published rebuttal; GEO-E022 shows lime plus diatomaceous earth forms exactly such a gel at room temperature from materials plausibly available in Egypt; GEO-E012 reports Si–Ca–Mg ratios absent from all six candidate quarries and hydrated phases not known to hydrate in nature, and those specific ratios have not been reproduced in natural stone by any record here. At Pumapunku, GEO-E006/GEO-E007 report organic matter inside dense andesite in peer-reviewed materials journals, and no independent analysis, blind comparison or dedicated rebuttal exists; GEO-E008 predates the analytical era and concerns a different lithology. Add the proponents' honest scope restriction (casing, tops and backing blocks only, per GEO-E023), the valid narrow form of GEO-C030 (a quarry match cannot see a binder, which at Khapia both sides concede), and the fact that the halite the natron recipe predicts is present (GEO-E030) with no bulk-versus-surface test run, and a proponent can say without error that the negative literature refuted the 1980s recipe and then stopped.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least one major megalithic monument contains man-made cast stone: blocks produced on site by binding processed mineral inputs (geopolymer, natron/waterglass, lime-pozzolan, or related chemistry) rather than by carving natural rock alone. The two concrete instances are casing and backing blocks of the Great Pyramid and the andesite and sandstone blocks of Pumapunku/Tiwanaku.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether anomalies exist — a measured quarrying rate, halite on the pyramid's inner walls, proponent SEM and NMR findings — and not over the salt, which both accounts predict once halite is native to Giza limestone and which fails as a discriminator on the present record. The Egyptian instance is contradicted on the record as tested; the residual disagreement there is whether the negative petrography, built around an alkali recipe, also excludes the calcium-silicate binder the pro-casting side has moved to, and whether the disputed samples were the right physical objects. The live disagreement is Andean: whether the organic matter and microstructures one team reports in Pumapunku andesite would survive an independent, blinded comparison against natural volcanic rock — the same audit that, at Giza, turned claimed casting signatures into ordinary geology — and whether Cerro Khapia yielded dressed blocks or natural sand.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the Andes, where the case verdict now turns: a desk check of the Iwawe Stratum V deposit and the piedras cansadas against the excavators' own descriptions; a survey of Cerro Khapia for extraction faces versus natural sand; and independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite with a natural andesite control and criteria fixed in advance. For Egypt: an independent laboratory testing provenance-secure casing stone specifically for a calcium-silicate binder against matched Tura limestone; and a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many blocks against a Mokattam natural-limestone remanence baseline, which tests set-in-place versus quarried-and-rotated regardless of recipe. For the salt: XRD of efflorescence on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock and Tura quarry faces, which would close the line if positive; and the remaining medieval authors for the al-Maʾmūn report. Either direction is decisive for the specific monument.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Quarrying, carving, and transport with well-attested means: dolerite pounders and copper tools, fire-setting, ramps, sledges, levers, and large organized labor forces. This is supported by unfinished monuments abandoned mid-carve at quarries, tool marks and tools at extraction sites, worker settlements, experimental carving, and geochemical provenance matching such as Stone 58 to West Woods. Direct petrography of pyramid stone shows sedimentary bedding, fossils, and tectonic fractures that moulds do not produce, and a genuine geopolymer control shows what a binder looks like when present. Salt on interior walls is halite, which effloresces at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites and is reported as a primary sedimentary constituent of Giza limestone, mobilised by humidity and visitor-driven condensation. Slow measured pounding rates imply more labour or supplementary techniques, not manufacture. At Pumapunku, the andesite comes from Cerro Khapia as dressed blocks, and the organic and glassy phases reported are natural to volcanic rock. The account's gaps are quantitative, not existential.

components.label: Egyptian attribution: Great Pyramid blocks cast (GEO-C020)
components.note: Four non-proponent petrographic studies read the stone as natural; GEO-E020's positive control shows a casting binder is detectable when present and absent here. Residual objection: the C–S–H binder of GEO-E017 is untested by those negatives; sample identity disputed.

components.label: Andean attribution: Pumapunku andesite and sandstone cast (GEO-C021, GEO-C004, GEO-C903)
components.note: The only direct laboratory records on the stone (GEO-E006/E007) read it as artificial and nothing tests them directly; but one team, contested custody, no blind criteria, and the Giza precedent of non-diagnostic SEM features. Checkable at Iwawe and Khapia.

components.label: Feasibility and ingredients (GEO-C012, GEO-C010, GEO-C011, GEO-C013)
components.note: Natron supply established; artificial limestone demonstrably makeable; temperatures plausible on declared priors. Feasibility is not occurrence and carries little diagnostic weight.

components.label: The salt line as evidence of natron chemistry (GEO-C003, GEO-C506, GEO-C906, GEO-C907)
components.note: Halite on chamber walls is confirmed but occurs at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and is reported native to Giza limestone; the medieval salt report has no traceable source. Bedrock efflorescence test (GEO-R010) would close it.

components.label: Methods critiques (GEO-C030, GEO-C594)
components.note: Trace-element quarry matching cannot see a binder (correct, and decisive at Khapia); XRD and binder-aware petrography can (so the claim overreaches). Undocumented restoration is a real confound at Giza; its generality awaits audit.

components.label: Aswan quarrying anomalies (GEO-C001, GEO-C002, GEO-C006, GEO-C502)
components.note: One peer-reviewed rate measurement stresses the pounders-only account; the rest is proponent anecdote. Bears on the completeness of the orthodoxy, not on casting.

researchPriority.reason: The flagship instance is contradicted on the record and the cheap decisive tests for the surviving Andean branch (GEO-R009 desk check of Iwawe Stratum V; GEO-R012 Khapia survey) and for the salt (GEO-R010) cost little and would move the case verdict in either direction. Information per unit cost is high for those items; the ceiling is moderate because the hypothesis's best-tested branch has already failed and its remaining support is a single non-independent line.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Existential thesis graded branch by branch. The Egyptian instance is contradicted (GEO-E018, E019, E020, E021 against E012, E017). The Andean instance has supporting records on the stone itself (GEO-E006/E007) and no direct negative; GEO-E008 is on sandstone with 1971 methods and cannot exclude same-quarry aggregate, and GEO-E009 (Stonehenge provenance) cannot exclude it either. One contradicted instance does not refute an existential claim; one untested, non-independent positive of a type shown non-diagnostic elsewhere does not support it. The decisive test has not been run where the claim now lives.

treatment.plainLanguage: Somewhere, at least one great stone monument contains blocks that were manufactured like concrete rather than cut from natural rock.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis; if true it decides the case outright against the carved-and-transported account for that monument.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every monument stone examined by anyone outside the proponent camp has read as natural, and the one positive-control study showed the features proponents call artificial occur in undisputed quarry stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent, provenance-secure re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite against a natural andesite control reproducing — or dissolving — the organic and microstructural findings
A targeted test for a calcium-silicate binder in provenance-secure Great Pyramid casing stone, positive or null
Iwawe Stratum V and Cerro Khapia turning out to be natural sand store and sand source — or dressing debris and quarry faces
A blinded paleomagnetic survey of pyramid blocks against a Mokattam remanence baseline

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E020 is decisive for the recipe tested: with a genuine Davidovits geopolymer as positive control, the Na+K/Al binder enrichment and air-void matrix a real casting binder leaves are absent from every casing stone, and the Si-rich spheres of GEO-E012 occur in natural limestone too. GEO-E018 adds in-situ bedding, burrows, fossil cross-sections and block-confined tectonic fractures across many blocks; GEO-E019 finds the showcase Lauer sample natural; GEO-E021 finds a museum casing fragment natural with opal-CT rather than synthetic cristobalite. GEO-E033 removes the salt as support. Against: GEO-E012 (contested provenance) and GEO-E017 (one stone, Barsoum co-author, unrebutted). Confidence moderate because the sample-identity dispute is unresolved and the C–S–H binder of GEO-E017 lies outside GEO-E020's test.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the Great Pyramid's blocks — casing, tops and backing, not the core — were made from reconstituted limestone rather than quarried.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true it establishes the thesis at its most famous site; on the present record it is the best-tested instance and it fails.
treatment.strongestObjection: The 2011 NMR reading of a Bent Pyramid casing stone as Tura grains in a calcium-silicate gel has no published rebuttal, and none of the negative studies tested for that binder.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent lab finding a calcium-silicate cement in provenance-secure casing stone absent from matched Tura limestone
Resolution of the Lauer-sample identity dispute in the proponents' favour together with a binder signature on the authentic piece
A blinded paleomagnetic survey finding a shared present-field remanence across many blocks

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 are the only records that examine the monument stone and they read it as artificial; GEO-E036 restates them. Nothing in the ledger tests them directly: GEO-E008 attributes the red sandstone to natural quarries with 1971 methods and neither examines the andesite nor can exclude same-quarry aggregate (GEO-C030, GEO-E035). The support is thin because the two papers are one team and one sample set, custody is contested, criteria were never blind-tested, volcanic rocks host organic and glassy phases naturally, and SEM features of this kind proved non-diagnostic at Giza under a positive control (GEO-E020). No evidence at all supports the sandstone half.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the andesite and red sandstone blocks at Pumapunku and Tiwanaku were cast from a mineral paste rather than carved.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true it establishes the thesis; it is the branch on which the case verdict now turns.
treatment.strongestObjection: The identical class of evidence — electron-microscope features read as artificial — was checked against a genuine geopolymer at Giza and turned out to occur in natural rock; that check has never been run on andesite, and the only people who have looked are the hypothesis's authors.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite with a natural andesite control and pre-registered criteria
Documentation of Iwawe Stratum V as natural andesite sand dated to construction, or as dressing debris
Quarry faces and en-route carved ashlars on Cerro Khapia, or their absence

claimAssessments.reasoning: A reporting claim: GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 record two peer-reviewed papers (Materials Letters, Ceramics International) that report organic matter and microstructural features their authors argue are inconsistent with natural volcanic stone. The citations are confirmed; the source records show the content was characterised via the Davidovits 2024 bibliography rather than read directly, which stops the grade short of established. The correctness of the interpretation is graded in GEO-C021, not here.

treatment.plainLanguage: Peer-reviewed papers exist that report organic matter and unusual microstructures in Pumapunku andesite and argue they are not natural.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The reports are the case's only laboratory evidence from a disputed monument that reads as artificial; whether the features actually discriminate cast from natural andesite has not been tested, and the Giza precedent says such features may not.
treatment.strongestObjection: Same team and sample set as the attribution they support; volcanic rocks host glassy and organic phases naturally; no blind comparison against natural andesite was run.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Direct reading of the two papers showing the ledger characterisation is inaccurate
An independent replication or a dedicated published rebuttal

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E035 quotes the proponents' 2020 abstract stating each element: natural sand-consistency andesite from Cerro Khapia, storage at Iwawe Stratum V per Isbell & Burkholder 2002, and non-use of the quadrangular piedras cansadas. A descriptive claim about the model, directly supported by its primary statement. Not established because only the abstract was read (the PDF returned 403) and the venue is the proponents' own journal.

treatment.plainLanguage: The proponents' current recipe for Pumapunku says the builders used natural volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia, stored at a lakeshore village, and never used the famous abandoned blocks.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Does not itself decide the thesis, but converts the Andean claim into checkable predictions — a deposit, a mountain, and some abandoned blocks — that separate it from the orthodox account where geochemistry cannot.
treatment.strongestObjection: The model concedes that both accounts place the andesite's origin at Khapia, so it also concedes that the strongest conventional evidence class cannot test it; its predictions are untested and the abandoned blocks it disowns are documented on the transport route.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the full 2020 paper and finding the model stated differently
Isbell & Burkholder's own description of Stratum V

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim bundles a true proposition with a false one. True: PXRF and ICP-MS do not see H, C or O, so a trace-element quarry match cannot distinguish carved quarry stone from stone cast with aggregate from that quarry (GEO-E024; conceded by both sides at Khapia, GEO-E035; limits GEO-E009). False: XRD is listed among the blind methods, yet XRD reads crystalline phases and is how GEO-E018 searched for zeolite cement. Overreach: GEO-E020's positive control shows binder-aware petrography detects a casting binder when present, so the blindness does not extend to the direct examinations of monument stone. Fóti's own table also misstates NMR.

treatment.plainLanguage: Matching a stone's trace elements to a quarry tells you where the rock came from, not whether it was carved or crushed and re-bound.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Does not decide the thesis but limits what one class of conventional evidence can prove; in its narrow form it is why Pumapunku cannot be settled by geochemistry, while in its broad form it fails against the petrography.
treatment.strongestObjection: The critique does not touch GEO-E018–E021, which examined the stone itself with methods that see binders, and Jana's positive control demonstrates the signature is visible when real.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A methods audit (GEO-R003) showing binder-aware measurements were in fact part of the major provenance attributions
Demonstration that a low-percentage binder evades SEM-EDS as well as bulk chemistry

claimAssessments.reasoning: A real artificial limestone exists in the record — the geopolymer block GEO-E020 used as its positive control — and GEO-E022 shows the C–S–H chemistry forms at room temperature from lime and diatomaceous earth. GEO-E013's multi-ton demonstration blocks are self-reported and never independently analysed, so the 'large' and 'ancient inputs only' components rest on proponent report. GEO-E012 concerns disputed monument samples and is not a feasibility trial.

treatment.plainLanguage: It is possible to make big, hard, convincing-looking limestone blocks from limestone rubble and a binder using ingredients ancient people had.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Necessary for the thesis but nearly silent on it: feasibility is not occurrence, and modern production knowledge does not establish ancient practice.
treatment.strongestObjection: No independently documented large-block replication using only specified ancient materials and operations exists; the only analysed artificial block was distinguishable from natural stone under the microscope.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent analysis of a demonstration block (its size, hardness, and whether the recipe used only ancient-available inputs)
A documented failure to scale the chemistry beyond hand samples

claimAssessments.reasoning: The ledger holds one weak proponent record (GEO-E016), a citation of Badari glassmaking whose dating and temperature basis are unverified; on the ledger alone the grade would be weakly_supported. The verdict rests on a declared prior — charcoal with forced draught reaching roughly 850 °C is uncontroversial for Bronze Age copper smelting, pottery and glass — stated here as such. The claim concerns achievable temperature, not sustained industrial-scale heat-work.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient builders could reach the roughly 850 °C that natron-based stone chemistry needs using charcoal and bellows.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Necessary background for the natron route; decides nothing, since the same pyrotechnology served metal and glass and says nothing about stone.
treatment.strongestObjection: Crucible-scale temperature attainment does not establish the fuel logistics of processing monument-scale tonnages.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Verification of the Badari precedent
Any record quantifying fuel demand for the proposed process at monument scale

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E010 (Shortland et al. 2006, mainstream peer-reviewed archaeological science) identifies Wadi el Natrun and al-Barnuj as the primary ancient natron sources for the vitreous industries and documents the 7th–9th-century decline and replacement by plant ash; GEO-E011 supplies the compositional criterion behind such timelines. Nothing in the ledger contests it and the claim's wording tracks the source.

treatment.plainLanguage: Egypt had large natron deposits that were mined from ancient times, and the supply fell away in the early medieval period.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes ingredient availability and a supply discontinuity; the paper concerns glass and faience and carries no implication for stone-making.
treatment.strongestObjection: None against the deposits and chronology; the exploitation is attested for glass, faience and mummification, not for structural stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A revision of the Shortland chronology by mainstream archaeological science

claimAssessments.reasoning: One weak supporting record (GEO-E015): an unattributed anecdote in a proponent book, flagged as under-sourced, with no controlled replication (GEO-R007 open). No undermining record. Ash-carbonation cementation is chemically plausible in principle (declared prior), but 'hardened artificial stone' is a stronger claim than plausibility grants.

treatment.plainLanguage: A fire pit used for years can accidentally turn its ash into something stone-like, which might be how people first noticed stone could be made.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A discovery story; even if replicated it would show a pathway, not ancient practice.
treatment.strongestObjection: A single unattributed anecdote with no material characterisation.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A controlled long-cycle fire-pit replication with periodic material testing (GEO-R007), positive or null

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E001 directly reports the photogrammetric result — 216 cm³/h at 85 strikes per minute — from a peer-reviewed study whose figure and conclusion were confirmed against the paper. The claim is a measurement report, so one well-described experiment carries it. Short of established because it is a single team, granite and tool configuration with no replication (GEO-R002), and the claim's generic phrasing invites extrapolation the one measurement cannot support.

treatment.plainLanguage: When scientists measured it carefully, hitting granite with a dolerite pounder removed only about a cupful of rock per hour.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Stresses the pounders-only timeline for the Aswan obelisk; casting is only one of several ways to absorb the shortfall (fire-setting, chisels, more labour), so it barely discriminates.
treatment.strongestObjection: Skilled ancient crews with maintained tools, better posture or fire-setting assistance may have far exceeded a modern experimental rate.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent replication with sensitivity to technique, tool mass and granite type returning a substantially higher rate

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E003 is a proponent's anecdote: attempt counts, cumulative effort and wear on the test block are all unquantified, and nothing has been surveyed. GEO-E002 supplies only context. No undermining record, but the support is the thinnest kind.

treatment.plainLanguage: Tourists have been hitting a test block at Aswan with ancient pounders for decades and nobody is reported to have made a scoop mark.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Untrained visitors striking briefly is not a test of a trained crew working for weeks; even if true it says nothing about casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Unquantified, unsurveyed anecdote; casual strikes are not comparable to sustained skilled labour.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A survey of the test block for wear and any count of attempts
A documented scoop mark produced by trained experimenters

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E005 is a proponent's verbal description; shaft dimensions have not been independently surveyed and the biomechanical assertion is untested. No undermining record. The catalog carries a competing proponent reading of the same features (GEO-C536), which bears on what they would mean, not on whether they are as described.

treatment.plainLanguage: Deep narrow shafts beside the obelisk look too tight for anyone to swing a hammer-stone at the bottom.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: At most a puzzle for the pounding orthodoxy; wedging, fire-setting, or abrasion from above with hafted tools would each answer it without casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Unsurveyed; ancient quarry workings routinely include features cut by methods not obvious to a modern observer.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent survey of the shafts' dimensions and tool marks

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E002 records the characterisation of Engelbach's method — one self-conducted hour, no mass measured, count-divided-by-four — but the record's own limitation says it is taken from Fóti and not verified against the 1922/1923 texts, and the SRC-FOTI-2024 record notes three other Fóti characterisations found to differ from their sources. Plausible and directionally corroborated by the source's reliability note, but resting on an unverified second-hand account.

treatment.plainLanguage: The textbook story that Aswan granite was quarried by pounding rests on a 1922 report whose own experiment was one man for one hour.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Weakens the pedigree of the orthodox rate, not its truth; a thin original basis is compatible with the orthodoxy being right.
treatment.strongestObjection: Engelbach's interpretation is corroborated by abundant contextual field evidence — thousands of pounders, quarry trenches and scoop-mark morphology — regardless of how thin his own trial was.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the 1922 monograph and 1923 companion volume and confirming or correcting the characterisation

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only affirmative carrier is an uncited proponent web page (GEO-E004, GEO-E029) that also misdates the breach to 820 against the translator's 832 (GEO-E028). GEO-E027 finds that al-Suyūṭī's compilation of the principal medieval accounts describes the breach twice in detail — fire, vinegar, tools, catapults, the twenty-cubit wall, the dinars, the well, the granite basin with worn rope — and mentions no salt or coating. The claim that the accounts report salt is therefore against the accounts that have been read. Confidence low because the absence is within one compilation; al-Maqrīzī's full chapter, ʿAbd al-Laṭīf and the Vyse extracts remain unread (GEO-R001).

treatment.plainLanguage: Medieval Arabic accounts are said to describe salt-coated walls inside the pyramid when the caliph's men broke in; the accounts that have been read describe no such thing.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if a source were found, halite native to Giza limestone (GEO-C906) means a salt-coated wall is what quarried stone would produce too.
treatment.strongestObjection: Not every relevant Arabic source has been examined; a single located passage would revive the report.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A named medieval author, work and passage reporting salt on the chamber walls
Completion of the GEO-R001 reading list without finding one

claimAssessments.reasoning: The presence half is confirmed instrumentally (GEO-E030: halite by XRD and SEM-EDX), but the claim's content is the comparison — that comparable natural limestone monuments do not exhibit the salt — and that fails: GEO-E031 documents halite efflorescence at the Sphinx (carved Giza bedrock), Saqqara, the White Monastery and the Imni tomb, and GEO-E032 reports halite as a primary constituent of Giza nummulitic limestone. GEO-E026's comparator (European cathedrals) is the wrong lithology and climate. Confidence moderate because no concentration comparison or bulk-versus-surface test exists (GEO-R010).

treatment.plainLanguage: The Great Pyramid's stones are salty in a way ordinary limestone buildings are not — except that other Egyptian limestone monuments, including the Sphinx, are salty too.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both the natron recipe and quarrying of a salt-bearing marine limestone predict salt in the blocks; an observation both accounts predict cannot decide between them.
treatment.strongestObjection: Nobody has measured salt concentrations in pyramid stone against unworked quarry faces or tested whether the chloride is bulk-distributed rather than surface efflorescence.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: XRD of efflorescence on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock and Tura quarry faces finding no halite
Bulk chlorine in cored pyramid stone far exceeding matched natural limestone

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E030 quotes the peer-reviewed Sessa et al. 2026 paper, read in full via its open-access copy: XRD of seven samples 'confirmed the presence of only halite, calcite, and quartz', SEM-EDX of the efflorescence detected only Na and Cl, no nitrates, no widespread gypsum. The claim is scoped to what the paper reports about its samples.

treatment.plainLanguage: Modern laboratory analysis shows the white crust on the pyramid's inner chamber walls is ordinary salt, plus the stone's own calcite and quartz.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Confirms the salt is NaCl; carries no weight toward casting because the same paper reads the halite as native to the limestone.
treatment.strongestObjection: XRD detection limit is around 5 wt%, so minor sulfate phases could be present undetected; only efflorescence and detached fragments were analysed, no cores.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A correction or retraction of the Sessa et al. results

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E032 reproduces Sessa et al.'s citation of Klemm & Klemm for halite as the primary salt within the Giza nummulitic limestone strata, 'likely precipitated from evaporating marine or lagoonal waters', and adds the authors' own finding of Na and Cl in visually unaffected detached fragments read as inherent to the matrix. Second-hand transmission — Klemm & Klemm 2010 and Hemeda & Sonbol 2020 were not read — and an inference from fragments rather than cores, so provisional; a marine-evaporite halite phase in a nummulitic limestone is geologically ordinary, which makes the citation credible.

treatment.plainLanguage: Salt is a natural part of the Giza plateau's limestone, laid down when the rock formed in an evaporating ancient sea.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The record that neutralises the salt line: if halite is native to the source rock, salt on the blocks is expected under carving and stops being evidence for natron chemistry.
treatment.strongestObjection: The primary geological source has not been read for this case, and 'inherent' rests on detached fragments, not cored bedrock.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading Klemm & Klemm 2010 directly and finding the statement absent or qualified
Efflorescence sampling on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock (GEO-R010) finding no halite

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E034 supplies a concrete instance at the flagship monument: 1995–97 cleaning and cavity-filling inside the Khufu pyramid with no available documentation, a sulfur-rich modern fill detectable on the wall, and salt efflorescence re-forming extensively within two years. That establishes the confound at Giza. The claim's general quantifier ('almost no megalithic site') is not tested by one monument and awaits the audit (GEO-R005).

treatment.plainLanguage: Most ancient sites have been cleaned, patched and restored without anyone writing down what was done, so a strange-looking surface could be modern work.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A confound rather than a discriminator: it lowers the weight of every surface argument in either direction, including the proponents' taste tests and any veneer or tooling claim.
treatment.strongestObjection: One documented gap does not establish universality; some conservation programmes publish meticulous records.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A systematic cross-site restoration audit showing complete histories exist for the key disputed sites

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E014 records that Fóti has argued the Rekhmire scene fits mineral or waterglass processing better than bronze casting, which is what the claim as worded asserts. No independent iconographic, inscriptional or residue evidence adjudicates the reading, and conventional Egyptology has not engaged it. The merit of the reinterpretation, rather than the fact that it has been made, is where doubt lives and is graded through diagnosticity and confidence.

treatment.plainLanguage: A famous tomb painting of workers casting metal has been re-read by a proponent as showing mineral processing instead.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An untested interpretive argument against a conventional reading backed by abundant independent evidence for New Kingdom bronze work; even if the scene showed mineral processing, it would not show stone casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: No prediction of either reading — residues, tools, inscriptions — has been checked against the archaeological record.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A joint Egyptology and history-of-technology re-examination (GEO-R008) finding the apparatus or inscriptions inconsistent with bronze work — or confirming them
